System lubricating oil serves the consum: System lubricating oil serves the consumers specified for the engine. Crosshead engines may have separate cylinder lubrication, and a turbocharger may have a separate or common supply. Use the maker-approved oil grade and sampling programme. Investigate water, fuel dilution, abnormal viscosity and wear-metal trends against operating conditions and maker limits.
The Chief Officer checks each liferaft f: The Chief Officer checks each liferaft float-free arrangement against the approved raft and hydrostatic release unit instructions. Connect the painter through the specified weak link to the correct strong point. Do not confuse the retaining lashing with the painter or add lashings that prevent release. Check capacity and distribution against the approved life-saving appliance plan and persons on board.
When mooring winches operate together, t: When mooring winches operate together, the Chief Officer coordinates the stations and avoids conflicting movements and excessive line loads. Commands identify the line and action, are repeated back and are followed by completion reports. In danger, give the agreed stop command, stop the equipment safely and re-establish communication before restarting.
The Chief Officer leads the forward anch: The Chief Officer leads the forward anchoring station. The Master assesses water depth including tide, hawse-pipe height, available cable, holding ground, weather, current, swinging room and equipment limits. There is no universal formula converting depth directly into a safe number of shackles. Walking back or letting go depends on the approved procedure and windlass capability, not one universal depth threshold.
While cable is paid out, report its leng: While cable is paid out, report its length, direction and observed load to the bridge. Brought up means the vessel has come to rest on its cable; it does not guarantee continued holding. The bridge verifies position and movement and maintains a watch for dragging using independent observations.
At anchor, maintain the planned watch us: At anchor, maintain the planned watch using suitable independent position and movement checks. Compare observations with the expected swinging area and conditions. Report suspected dragging and worsening weather promptly to the Master. Prepare propulsion and assess available responses under the ship-specific anchoring and emergency procedures.
The cadet learns how a passage plan prov: The cadet learns how a passage plan provides contingency options: abort points before committing to a critical manoeuvre, suitable emergency anchoring areas, boundaries around hazards and responses to propulsion or navigation-system failure. Confirm that the options remain feasible as traffic, weather, tide and equipment status change.
The engine cadet learns bridge–engine co: The engine cadet learns bridge–engine communication through the telegraph, engineer call and talkback systems. Observe how the team receives and acknowledges a crash-astern demand and applies the installation-specific response. Such a demand is an operational event, not an exercise to initiate without authority.
The emergency fire-pump test follows the: The emergency fire-pump test follows the approved procedure: start the pump, establish suction through its priming arrangement where required, pressurise the fire main and verify the specified delivery at the designated hydrants. Priming removes air or establishes the required suction condition; it is not determined by a pump being foreign-made. Record and report any failure.
Apply the rope maker’s retirement criter: Apply the rope maker’s retirement criteria and the ship’s mooring-line management plan. Consider construction, abrasion, cuts, internal damage, heat, chemicals and service history. Do not use a universal percentage of damaged fibres for every line. Identify and segregate suspect lines and report them to the Chief Officer.
On the order to stand by for mooring or: On the order to stand by for mooring or unmooring, the Bosun briefs the station team and prepares the planned lines and leads. Inspect fairleads, rollers and equipment, test winches under the approved procedure, confirm communication and lighting, and wear the required protective equipment. Keep personnel clear of bights and potential line recoil paths.
Pass a suitable heaving line to the shor: Pass a suitable heaving line to the shore team only when the receiving area is clear. A monkey’s fist must contain rope only: do not add metal, sand or other weights. Use any alternative throwing aid only if approved. After the mooring line is received and secured as ordered, check its lead and report the line status.
Mooring winch controls permit heaving, p: Mooring winch controls permit heaving, paying out and braking. Operate only on an understood command identifying the line and action. Automatic-tension operation can move a line unexpectedly and alter load sharing; use it only under the approved mooring arrangement and operating instructions.
At the anchoring station, repeat back th: At the anchoring station, repeat back the required operation and cable length. Read the actual shackle markings and report cable direction, load and length accurately, for example two shackles in the water. Distinguish heaving, walking back and letting go; do not substitute an ambiguous command.
The able seafarer prepares the whistle,: The able seafarer prepares the whistle, day shapes and signalling equipment as directed by the officer of the watch. Give the appropriate manoeuvring, restricted-visibility or anchoring signals under that officer’s control and the applicable rules. Know the equipment location and operation; signal selection is not inferred from an informal deck command.
Forward and aft stations maintain clear: Forward and aft stations maintain clear radio communication with the bridge. Commands such as Send the head line ashore, Heave on the spring, Slack away the breast, Make fast and Let go must identify the intended line and action. Repeat back, act only when understood and report completion. A breast line is not the anchoring report up and down.
Before the manoeuvre, prepare the statio: Before the manoeuvre, prepare the station according to the mooring plan: arrange lines safely, check leads and equipment, prepare the heaving line and confirm communication. Remove slip and trip hazards and plan safe standing positions. Preparation does not authorise releasing a loaded line without an order.
When using a warping drum, follow the ma: When using a warping drum, follow the manufacturer’s instructions for the rope, number of turns and tail handling. There is no universal three-or-four-turn rule. Keep hands and clothing clear, avoid riding turns and never reach into a loaded or moving line. Stop and make the equipment and line safe before clearing a problem.
An automatic-tension winch can heave or: An automatic-tension winch can heave or pay out as its control responds to load. This can cause unexpected line movement and change the mooring arrangement. Select the permitted operating mode under the approved instructions, brief the team and keep personnel clear of the line and equipment.
Secure a mooring line on the designated: Secure a mooring line on the designated bitts using the approved arrangement for that line and fitting. Confirm the lead, load and required ability to release or adjust it. Do not add an improvised locking turn that prevents controlled release. Keep clear of loaded turns and follow the station leader’s instructions.
The able seafarer assists with windlass: The able seafarer assists with windlass operation and cable-length reporting under the station leader. Confirm the anchor, method and cable length before letting go or walking back. Read the ship’s markings rather than assuming a nominal shackle length. Use the brake and chain stopper according to the installation’s approved procedure.
When weighing anchor, report cable direc: When weighing anchor, report cable direction and load, up and down when the cable is vertical, and anchor aweigh when it is clear of the bottom. Report excessive strain or windlass difficulty immediately. The bridge coordinates vessel movement; the station must not improvise a response that overloads the gear.
Do not release, pay out or heave a moori: Do not release, pay out or heave a mooring line without an understood instruction, except for the agreed immediate stop response to danger. During single-up, identify which lines remain loaded before changing the arrangement. Repeat back orders and report completion so the bridge can coordinate the manoeuvre.
Inspect ropes for abrasion, cuts, intern: Inspect ropes for abrasion, cuts, internal damage, heat or friction damage, chemical exposure and deterioration. Assess findings against the maker’s criteria and service history; identify and withdraw suspect equipment as required. Store ropes clean and protected from damaging surfaces, contamination and unsuitable environmental conditions.
Enclosed-space entry requires risk asses: Enclosed-space entry requires risk assessment, isolation, ventilation, representative atmospheric testing and an authorised permit to work (PTW). A safe oxygen reading alone does not exclude toxic or flammable gases. Use suitable calibrated instruments and the approved acceptance limits, maintain communications and an attendant, and have a practised rescue plan. Never enter impulsively to rescue a casualty. SOLAS III/19.3.3 requires crew with entry or rescue duties to participate in entry and rescue drills at least every two months.
A fast rescue boat (FRB) and its launchi: A fast rescue boat (FRB) and its launching appliance have approved operating limits. Assess weather, ship movement, boat condition and crew readiness before launch or recovery. Constant-tension or shock-absorbing arrangements reduce some recovery loads but do not make every sea state safe. Recovery is a critical part of the man-overboard (MOB) plan; follow the installation instructions and trained procedure.
Low-location lighting marks approved esc: Low-location lighting marks approved escape routes near deck level when higher signs are obscured. Applicable SOLAS requirements, FSS Code chapter 11 and IMO resolution A.752(18) govern the arrangement. Check the approved plan, condition, visibility and power or photoluminescent performance; ordinary decorative lighting is not a substitute.
On a steam-turbine LNG carrier, boil-off: On a steam-turbine LNG carrier, boil-off gas (BOG) from the LNG cargo can supply the boilers. The boiler, turbine, condenser and feed pump form the basic Rankine-cycle loop. Other LNG carriers use different propulsion arrangements; identify the actual installation before applying operating instructions.
On a man-overboard (MOB) alarm, raise th: On a man-overboard (MOB) alarm, raise the alarm, mark the position and maintain visual contact with dedicated lookouts. The bridge selects a recovery manoeuvre appropriate to when the casualty was seen, sea room, traffic and ship response. Prepare the approved recovery equipment and coordinate communications; a named turn is not automatically suitable for every situation.
A man-overboard (MOB) response combines: A man-overboard (MOB) response combines an immediate alarm, suitable flotation and marking aids, continuous lookout, position marking and a coordinated recovery plan. Use the rescue boat only when appropriate within its approved launch and recovery limits. Assess other available recovery means. Cold-water exposure makes delay dangerous, but an unsafe launch can create further casualties.
Cylinder-oil feed rate and oil selection: Cylinder-oil feed rate and oil selection must follow the engine maker’s guidance for the fuel, engine condition and load. Interpret scrape-down oil base number (BN or TBN) with iron results, sampling consistency and inspection findings. Low residual alkalinity and high wear require investigation; high BN alone does not justify reducing feed rate. Use trends and maker action limits, not a universal BN target.
Plan realistic ship-specific fire, SOPEP: Plan realistic ship-specific fire, SOPEP spill-response and man-overboard (MOB) exercises under the applicable drill schedule. Include communication and equipment checks. Debrief each exercise, assign corrective actions and verify that weaknesses have been addressed.
Fire, man-overboard (MOB) and abandon-sh: Fire, man-overboard (MOB) and abandon-ship exercises practise assigned duties, muster, communications and correct use of survival equipment. Operate equipment and conduct launches under the applicable safe procedures. Record the debrief and follow up deficiencies.
Keep the muster list current and practis: Keep the muster list current and practise assigned fire, man-overboard (MOB), abandon-ship and enclosed-space rescue duties. Demonstrate rescue arrangements without exposing unprotected crew to a hazardous atmosphere. Record lessons and verify corrective actions.
